summary.text: 人 is a pictograph of a person in profile. Early examples use it for ‘person’; the whole graph depicts a figure rather than combining separate modern components.

formation.text: Pictographic: the graph depicts a person in profile. Descriptions interpret its strokes as a head, body, arm and legs; this explains the figure, not a proven stroke-by-stroke sequence. Two early graphic variants are described as equivalent in meaning, with one underlying the Small Seal form and the other developing through clerical writing into regular 人.

history.text: Oracle-bone, bronze, Chu-script and Small Seal materials are recorded. The selected oracle-style and seal-script illustrations are modern redrawings of forms in those traditions; they are examples, not evidence of a direct sequence of graphic change.

The Shuowen account describes 人 as depicting an arm and shin, consistent with interpreting the graph as a human figure. A separate account describes two early graphic variants as equivalent in meaning: one underlies the Small Seal form, while the other was common in clerical script and developed into regular 人. Some forms called ancient in later references are not attested in the early corpora checked and should not be treated as established ancestors.

uncertainties.text: The cited oracle-bone examples belong to that script tradition, but their individual dates and the character’s first-use date are not supplied.

Reports describe 人 used to write other graphs or words, including 夷 and 年, and separately describe 人 as a phonetic element within 年. The sound correspondences behind the reported whole-graph uses are not independently established here.

evidence.text: The legs of a human being
Pictograph of the side view of a person.
天地之性最貴者也。此籒文。象臂脛之形。凡人之屬皆从人。

Pictogram (象形) – side view of a standing man, highlighting an arm and a leg. Compare 大, 立 (lì), 卩, 夭, and 氏 according to one interpretation. See also the original version of 年.
亼 is similar but unrelated; it represents an open mouth flipped upside down and appears on top of characters such as 食, 金, 令, 龠, and 今.
It represents a roof in the characters 余, 茶, 舍, and 倉. It represents a flag on a flagpole in 㫃. Eventually, it represents two parallel mountain walls in 谷.
The stylized version to the left of the characters is 亻 (see also 千). Similar but unrelated to 彳.
Sagart (1999) relates it to Tibetan ཉེན (nyen, “relative”), from ཉེ (nye, “near”) + nominalizing suffix -n; if so, from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *nəj(ʔ) (“near”).
Schuessler (2007) proposes two etymologies:
* Same etymon as 仁 (OC *njin, “to be kind; to be good”), from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s/k-niŋ (“heart; brain; mind”). The semantic association of 仁 with 人 was somewhat late, dated to Mencius's time; later on, 仁 would be usually interpreted as "humane, acting like a human being".
** If so, semantically parallel with Tibetan སེམས་ཅན (sems can, “living being, human, animal”, literally “possessor of mind”); and Latin animalis (“living, having soul”) from anima (“soul”).
* Related to Proto-Mon-Khmer *ɲaʔ ~ *ɲah (“person”) with a nominalizing suffix -n, from the auto-ethnonym of a hostile, possibly Austroasiatic-speaking, eastern people, whom the Sinitic-speaking Shang referred to as 人方 (OC *njin paŋ).

The Min native word for “person”; used as a replacement character for 儂 /侬. It is historically attested for Hokkien in the Arte de la Lengua Chiõ Chiu (1620) and Dictionario Hispanico Sinicum (1626-1642). Use of 人 for Hokkien is recommended by Taiwan's Ministry of Education (ROC MOE).

evidence.field: 研訂瀏覽; historical-form claims and Mandarin reading
evidence.text: The entry quotes Shuowen’s explanation that 人 depicts arm and shin forms. It cautions that certain ancient forms reported in later references are not found in oracle-bone, bronze, or ancient Zhou-script materials, and says their evidence is unknown. It records modern Mandarin rén. This cautions against treating unsupported later-reported shapes as ancestors, but does not dispute the profile-person interpretation.

evidence.field: 人 entry; printed p. 698; PDF p. 711
evidence.text: The 人 entry identifies the graph as pictographic, resembling a person in side view, and gives its basic sense as ‘person.’ It describes two early graphic variants—one joining head-like and torso-like parts, another joining head-like and arm-like parts—as equivalent in meaning; it says the former underlies the Shuowen Small Seal form, while the latter was more common in clerical script and developed into regular 人. The attached scan visibly shows the 人 headword, the form sequence, and this explanation. The continuation on PDF p. 712 is the separate 仁 entry, not a continuation of 人.
evidence.title: 字源, 李學勤主編, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The record lists oracle-bone example 合集6175, bronze example 集成00944, Chu-script material, and Small Seal / Shuowen material. Its explanation reads 人 as a person standing in profile, interpreting the upper part as head, middle as body, an extended stroke as arm, and lower part as legs. This is the database’s graphic interpretation, not a separately demonstrated stroke chronology.
evidence.title: 漢字「人」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析; 人; shape and examples
evidence.text: The entry describes ancient 人 as a profile figure standing with hands lowered and gives its basic sense as person. It cites oracle-bone examples 《合集》22626 ‘伐十人’ and 《合集》20328 ‘余一人’ (royal self-reference); reports bronze uses glossed ‘common people,’ ‘people,’ and a ruler’s self-reference; and discusses particular uses of 人 for 夷 and 年. The cited loans are source assertions; this entry alone does not independently establish their phonological basis.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: The oldest forms are labelled oracle-bone and bronze forms in the paleographic database, but the inspected page does not date the individual cited specimens; the oracle-bone corpus context is broadly Late Shang, not a character-specific first-use date.
No independent external verification of the supplied Baxter–Sagart table row was possible, and no same-system comparison is needed for 人 itself because it has no proposed sound component.

The official character-specific Unihan endpoint https://www.unicode.org/cgi-bin/GetUnihanData.pl?codepoint=4EBA was attempted but inaccessible in the web tool. The local exact kMandarin row was supplied and retained as local metadata only; it is not represented as externally verified.

Shuowen’s account is an early historical explanation, not independent confirmation of a pristine pictorial origin. Inspected modern paleographic references support the side-profile human interpretation, but no glyph image was visually inspected in this research.

The source database offers selected older semantic uses, but not a systematic chronology of all extensions such as individual, people, someone, or other person. No chronology is inferred from modern gloss lists.

The reported 人-for-夷 and 人-for-年 loans are source assertions. Their precise early pronunciations and the phonological basis of each loan were not independently established in this search. No claim is made that 人 derives from 仁 or vice versa.
No individual date was found for cited oracle-bone specimen references; the sources classify them as oracle-bone material but do not supply a character-specific first-use date.

The sources identify the original sense as ‘person’ and provide Shang oracle-bone instances, then list later bronze and textual uses such as common people, people/population, and ruler’s self-reference. They do not provide a complete dated semantic chronology or prove every link between these uses.

The reported whole-graph loans 人-for-夷 and 人-for-年 are not independently phonologically established in the inspected evidence. The separate statement that 人 functions as 年’s phonetic element does not itself establish the sound basis for the whole-graph loan.

Shuowen’s explanation is preserved as a historical account, not independent proof. The inspected paleographic descriptions support a human profile interpretation; the Taiwan MOE entry warns that some forms later labelled ancient lack attestation in early corpora.

The character-specific Unicode Unihan endpoint failed to load. The local kMandarin and Baxter–Sagart rows remain local metadata; current reading metadata is not evidence of ancient sound relationships.
The selected historical glyphs are modern vector redrawings. The web tool could not fetch their SVG pixels, so no visual inspection is claimed.

[SCAN VERIFICATION REQUIRED] 字源, PDF p. 711 / printed p. 698, 人 entry’s historical glyph sequence: the attached scan was inspected and the prose/headword are readable, but the small individual glyph forms were not independently identified one by one; cite only the verified prose unless glyph identities are checked separately.
The cited oracle-bone and bronze specimens are identified by corpus references, but the inspected sources do not give individual specimen dates or establish the character’s first-use date.

The book and external records support early uses for person, people/common people, and royal self-reference, but do not provide a complete dated semantic chronology or demonstrate every semantic link.

Reports of 人 used for 夷 or 年 are not independently phonologically established in the inspected evidence. The claim that 人 serves as a phonetic element in 年 is distinct from the claim of whole-graph borrowing.
The official Unihan character-specific page was not opened in this invocation; supplied local kMandarin metadata is not used here as external evidence.
